newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Eurosceptic Swedes risk isolation over EMU.
newsitem.headline: Eurosceptic Swedes risk isolation over EMU.

text.p: Sweden's loose interpretation of the economic criteria for joining a European single currency threatens to isolate the country and brand it as a difficult customer in EU circles, leading economists said on Tuesday.

"Sweden agreed to join the EMU (European economic and monetary union), and it's going to break an agreement it has entered into. Of course we're going to be punished for it," economics professor Johan Lybeck said.

Swedish Prime Minister Goran Persson and Finance Minister Erik Asbrink have insisted on a unique degree of freedom in interpreting the economic convergence demands of the Maastricht Treaty that set out the framework for EMU.
The treaty demands that a country must peg its currency in the Exchange Rate Mechanism (ERM) for two years before it can join the single currency of the Economic and Monetary Union.

However, Persson and Asbrink have repeatedly maintained that the important thing is currency stability itself, arguing that the 15 percentage point fluctuation bands of the ERM do little to prove a currency is fit to be a part of EMU.
This view has found little support among Sweden's EU colleagues.
Alexandre Lamfalussy, president of the European Monetary Institute -- precursor to a European central bank -- said in Sweden on Monday the country would do well to play it by the book.

"My opinion is that a country should be in the ERM for two years before it can enter the EMU, and that's the interpretation of the majority (of countries) of the convergence criteria," Lamfalussy said.
This would imply pegging the crown in the ERM before the turn of the year, since the currency union is due to come into force on January 1, 1999.
Sweden's 1994 decision to join the European Union obliged it to adopt the single currency as soon as it fulfilled all of the convergence criteria, Lamfalussy said.
But Sweden's ruling Social Democrats insist the decision must be taken by the Swedish parliament -- which effectively means by the SDP party congress in September next year.
Economists said the issue was a political minefield.

"There is a risk here of course in that Sweden and Britain have adopted the same type of attitude. Politically, it's not possible for Sweden to enter the ERM at the moment, it's hugely unpopular among voters," Olle Djerf, chief economist at Sweden's Nordbanken said in an interview.

A recent poll funded by the European Commission showed Swedes to be the EU's most reluctant citizens. Just 32 percent of Swedes polled said they thought the EU was a good thing, while 36 percent said joining had been a bad move.
This Euro-scepticism has not gone unnoticed in Brussels.
Lisa Steneberg, head of the EU Commission's delegation in Sweden, recently said the country's tendency to complain had weakened its negotiating position on key issues.

With a general election due in September 1998, the SDP is hardly likely to do anything as widely unpopular as peg the crown to the ERM. But Lybeck said four more years of power would give Asbrink and Persson room for manouevre.
"They're playing a very difficult game but they're playing very skilfully. By not joining in 1999, the politicians can flex their muscles a bit. On the other hand, do they have a choice?" he asked.

"The ERM is an ante-chamber to the EMU, and by joining they'd be playing into the hands of the (anti-EMU) left. But I'm certain Sweden will join by 2002 when it's time to pool currencies," Lybeck said.
